questions.q: Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly of India?
questions.a: Rajendra Prasad|Dr Rajendra Prasad|Dr. Rajendra Prasad
questions.e: Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected President of the Constituent Assembly; Sachchidananda Sinha was only its temporary chairman at the first meeting.

questions.q: Members of the Constituent Assembly were elected indirectly by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies according to the scheme proposed by the ______.
questions.a: Cabinet Mission|Cabinet Mission Plan|British Cabinet Mission
questions.e: Under the Cabinet Mission scheme of 1946, seats were allotted to provinces roughly in proportion to their population.

questions.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy in the Indian Constitution were borrowed from the constitution of ______.
questions.e: The Irish Constitution provided the model for the Directive Principles of State Policy.

questions.q: The power of judicial review and the independence of the judiciary were borrowed from the constitution of the ______.
questions.e: From the US Constitution, India borrowed the charter of fundamental rights, judicial review and judicial independence.

questions.q: The Constituent Assembly of India took nearly three years to frame the Constitution.
p: (a) On 26 November of which year was the Constitution adopted?
(b) After the partition of the country, how many members remained in the Constituent Assembly?
(c) The idea of a federation with a strong central government was borrowed from which country's constitution?
Canada|Canadian
questions.e: The Assembly, reduced to 299 members after partition, adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949; the quasi-federal model came from Canada.

questions.q: The Right to Constitutional Remedies, which Dr Ambedkar called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution, is given in Article ______.
questions.e: Article 32 allows a citizen to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

questions.q: The writ which orders that an arrested person be produced before the court, so that the court can examine the legality of the arrest, is ______.
questions.e: Habeas corpus means 'to have the body'; the court can order release if the arrest is unlawful.

questions.q: Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden by Article ______.
questions.e: Article 17 abolishes untouchability, part of the Right to Equality.

questions.q: The writ issued when the court finds that an office holder is not performing a legal duty, ordering that the duty be done, is ______.
questions.e: Mandamus means 'we command'; quo warranto asks by what authority a person holds an office.

questions.q: The Right to Property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by which Constitutional Amendment in 1978? Write the number.
questions.e: The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the Right to Property from Fundamental Rights; it is now a legal right under Article 300A.

questions.q: The electoral system used for Lok Sabha elections, in which the candidate with the most votes wins, is called the ______ system.
questions.e: Under FPTP the candidate with more votes than any other wins, even without a majority of the votes cast.

questions.q: What is the minimum age to contest elections to the Lok Sabha?
questions.e: A candidate for the Lok Sabha or a State Assembly must be at least 25 years old; for the Rajya Sabha it is 30.

questions.q: The President and Vice-President of India are elected by proportional representation through the ______ system.
questions.e: Under the single transferable vote, voters rank candidates in order of preference and a winner needs a quota of votes.

questions.q: In which country, cited in the NCERT textbook, is the entire country treated as one constituency under proportional representation?
questions.e: In Israel parties get seats in the legislature in proportion to their national share of votes.

questions.q: Free and fair elections in India are conducted by an independent Election Commission.
p: (a) Which Article of the Constitution provides for the Election Commission?
(b) Who appoints the Chief Election Commissioner?
President|President of India|the President
(c) How many members, including the Chief Election Commissioner, does the Election Commission have at present?
questions.e: Article 324 sets up the Election Commission; it now has a CEC and two Election Commissioners, all appointed by the President.

questions.q: In India's parliamentary system, the nominal executive head of the country is the ______.
questions.e: The President is the nominal head; real executive power lies with the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers.

questions.q: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the ______.
questions.a: Lok Sabha|House of the People|lower house
questions.e: If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the whole Council of Ministers must resign.

questions.q: After the 91st Amendment (2003), the size of the Council of Ministers cannot exceed what percentage of the total members of the Lok Sabha?
questions.e: The 91st Amendment limits the Council of Ministers to 15 per cent of the Lok Sabha's (or Assembly's) strength.

questions.q: India has a parliamentary executive with a President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Council of Ministers.
p: (a) What is the term of office of the President, in years?
years
(b) Which Article of the Constitution allows President's Rule to be imposed in a state?
(c) Who is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
Vice-President|Vice President|Vice-President of India|Vice President of India
questions.e: The President serves five years; Article 356 provides for President's Rule; the Vice-President chairs the Rajya Sabha.

questions.q: Which body conducts recruitment of officers to the All India Services such as the IAS and IPS?
questions.e: The Union Public Service Commission recruits civil servants through competitive examinations.

questions.q: Members of the Rajya Sabha from a state are elected by the elected members of the ______.
questions.a: State Legislative Assembly|State Legislative Assemblies|Legislative Assembly|Vidhan Sabha|MLAs
questions.e: Rajya Sabha members are elected indirectly by MLAs, using the single transferable vote.

questions.q: How many members does the President nominate to the Rajya Sabha?
questions.e: The President nominates 12 members with special knowledge of literature, science, art and social service.

questions.q: The Rajya Sabha can delay a Money Bill for a maximum of how many days?
questions.e: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days.

questions.q: The anti-defection law was introduced by which Constitutional Amendment (1985)? Write the number.
questions.e: The 52nd Amendment (1985) disqualifies legislators who defect from the party on whose ticket they were elected.

questions.q: The time in Parliament, after Question Hour, when members can raise important matters without prior notice is popularly called ______.
questions.e: Zero Hour is not a formal rule but lets members raise urgent matters of public concern.

questions.q: Judges of the Supreme Court of India retire at the age of ______ years.
questions.e: Supreme Court judges retire at 65; they can be removed only by a special majority in both Houses of Parliament.

questions.q: A case filed in court by any person or group for the protection of public interest, even if they are not personally affected, is called ______.
questions.e: PIL relaxed the rule that only the aggrieved person can approach the court and became a main tool of judicial activism.

questions.q: In which 1973 case did the Supreme Court rule that Parliament cannot amend the basic structure of the Constitution?
questions.a: Kesavananda Bharati|Kesavananda Bharati case|Keshavananda Bharati|Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
questions.e: The Kesavananda Bharati judgment (1973) laid down the 'basic structure' doctrine limiting Parliament's power to amend.

questions.q: The Supreme Court of India is at the top of a single integrated judicial system.
p: (a) What is the maximum number of judges in the Supreme Court, including the Chief Justice, at present?
(b) The Supreme Court's power to give its opinion to the President on a question of law or fact is called its ______ jurisdiction.
advisory
(c) At what age do High Court judges retire?
years
questions.e: The Supreme Court has a sanctioned strength of 34 judges; it has advisory jurisdiction under Article 143; High Court judges retire at 62.

questions.q: The group of the Chief Justice and the senior-most judges of the Supreme Court that recommends names for the appointment of judges is called the ______.
questions.e: Through the collegium, senior judges play the main role in recommending appointments to the higher judiciary.

questions.q: Subjects like defence, foreign affairs and banking are in the ______ List.
questions.e: The Union List has subjects of national importance on which only Parliament can make laws.

questions.q: Education, forests and marriage are subjects in the ______ List.
questions.e: Both Parliament and state legislatures can make laws on Concurrent List subjects; Union law prevails in a conflict.

questions.q: Under the Indian Constitution, residuary powers, on subjects not mentioned in any list, lie with the ______.
questions.e: Residuary powers are given to the Union, showing the Constitution's tilt towards a strong centre.

questions.q: Which commission was appointed by the central government in 1983 to examine Centre-State relations?
questions.e: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) examined Centre-State relations and recommended that Article 356 be used sparingly.

questions.q: The 73rd Amendment (1992) deals with ______ local government.
questions.e: The 73rd Amendment deals with rural local bodies (Panchayati Raj); the 74th deals with urban local bodies.

questions.q: At least what proportion of seats in panchayats and municipalities is reserved for women?
questions.e: The 73rd and 74th Amendments reserve one-third of seats and of chairperson posts for women.

questions.q: Which committee recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj system in 1957?
questions.a: Balwant Rai Mehta|Balwantrai Mehta|Balwant Rai Mehta Committee
questions.e: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended elected local bodies at village, block and district levels.

questions.q: How many subjects are listed in the Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution for panchayats?
questions.e: The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects for panchayats; the Twelfth Schedule lists 18 for municipalities.

questions.q: 'Long Walk to Freedom' is the autobiography of ______.
questions.e: Mandela describes his struggle against apartheid in South Africa and his 27 years in prison (1962-1990).

questions.q: The 'harm principle', which allows society to restrict a person's freedom only to prevent harm to others, was given by ______ in 'On Liberty'.
questions.a: John Stuart Mill|J.S. Mill|JS Mill|J S Mill|Mill
questions.e: J.S. Mill distinguished self-regarding actions from other-regarding actions that may harm others.

questions.q: Freedom understood as the absence of external constraints, an area where the individual is left alone, is called ______ liberty.
questions.e: Negative liberty defines an inviolable area of non-interference; positive liberty concerns conditions that let people develop.

questions.q: Aung San Suu Kyi's well-known collection of writings on freedom is titled ______.
questions.e: In 'Freedom from Fear' she argues that true freedom means being free from fear of others' judgement and control.

questions.q: Policies such as reservation of seats, which aim to correct the effects of past inequality, are known as ______ action.
questions.e: Affirmative action gives special help to disadvantaged groups so that they can compete on equal terms.

questions.q: Granting equal citizenship and the right to vote to all citizens is an aspect of ______ equality.
questions.e: Political equality means equal citizenship rights, such as voting and freedom of expression.

questions.q: Which ideology holds that the root cause of inequality is private ownership of important economic resources such as land and factories?
questions.e: Marxists argue that inequality comes from private ownership of the means of production and seek public control of them.

questions.q: The principle that the same laws apply to everyone and no one is above the law is called the ______ of law.
questions.e: The rule of law, guaranteed by Article 14, means everyone, including those in power, is subject to the law.

questions.q: The Indian Constitution provides for ______ citizenship for the whole country.
questions.e: Unlike the USA, India has single citizenship; there is no separate state citizenship.

questions.q: Who wrote 'Citizenship and Social Class' (1950), defining citizenship as full membership of a community?
questions.e: T.H. Marshall described three kinds of citizenship rights: civil, political and social.

questions.q: People who are not citizens of any state are called ______ people.
questions.e: Stateless people lack the protection and rights of citizenship of any country, which creates serious problems for them.

questions.q: The Constitution and the Citizenship Act lay down who is a citizen of India and what equality citizens enjoy.
p: (a) Which Part of the Constitution deals with citizenship? Write the number.
(b) Citizenship can be acquired by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation or ______ of territory.
incorporation
(c) Which Article says the State shall not deny any person equality before the law?
questions.e: Part II (Articles 5-11) deals with citizenship; incorporation of territory is one way to acquire it; Article 14 guarantees equality before law.

questions.q: The Bolshevik (socialist) revolution in Russia, which led to the formation of the Soviet Union, took place in ______.
questions.e: The Bolshevik revolution of 1917 was inspired by socialist ideals and led to the formation of the Soviet system.

questions.q: The Soviet leader who introduced the reforms of perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness) was ______.
questions.e: Gorbachev became General Secretary in 1985 and tried to reform the Soviet system, which unleashed forces that led to its collapse.

questions.q: The Berlin Wall, a symbol of the Cold War division of Germany, was brought down by the people in ______.
questions.e: The Berlin Wall, built in 1961, fell in November 1989; Germany was reunified soon after.

questions.q: The model of sudden transition from an authoritarian socialist system to a democratic capitalist system in Russia, Central Asia and East Europe was called ______.
questions.e: Shock therapy, backed by the World Bank and IMF, involved rapid privatisation and led to economic ruin for many people.

questions.q: The Soviet Union disintegrated after a series of events that began in the late 1980s.
p: (a) In December of which year did the USSR disintegrate?
(b) Into how many independent republics did the USSR break up?
(c) Russia, Ukraine and Belarus formed which grouping to replace the USSR?
Commonwealth of Independent States|CIS
questions.e: In December 1991 the USSR broke into 15 independent countries; Russia, Ukraine and Belarus announced the Commonwealth of Independent States.

questions.q: ASEAN was established in ______ by five countries signing the Bangkok Declaration.
questions.e: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand set up ASEAN in 1967 to speed up economic growth and social progress.

questions.q: The European Union was established by the ______ Treaty signed in 1992.
questions.e: The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 created the EU, with a common foreign and security policy and later a common currency.

questions.q: China's 'open door' policy and economic reforms of 1978 were announced by ______.
questions.e: Deng Xiaoping's reforms opened China to foreign investment and technology, leading to very rapid growth.

questions.q: In which year did the United Kingdom hold the referendum in which a majority voted to leave the European Union?
questions.e: The UK voted to leave the EU in the 2016 referendum ('Brexit') and formally left in 2020.

questions.q: SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation) was set up in ______.
questions.e: SAARC was set up in 1985 by the South Asian countries to promote regional cooperation.

questions.q: Bangladesh, earlier East Pakistan, became an independent country in ______.
questions.e: After the war of December 1971, East Pakistan emerged as the independent country of Bangladesh.

questions.q: The Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan, brokered by the World Bank, was signed in ______.
questions.e: The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 has survived several conflicts between India and Pakistan.

questions.q: The militant organisation that fought for a separate Tamil Eelam in Sri Lanka was the ______.
questions.a: LTTE|Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam|Tamil Tigers
questions.e: The LTTE waged an armed struggle for a separate Tamil state; it was militarily defeated in 2009.

questions.q: Nepal abolished its monarchy and became a federal democratic republic in ______.
questions.e: After the 2006 people's movement, the Constituent Assembly abolished the monarchy in 2008; a new constitution followed in 2015.

questions.q: The United Nations was founded in ______ after the Second World War.
questions.e: The UN was founded on 24 October 1945 as a successor to the League of Nations.

questions.q: How many permanent members does the UN Security Council have?
questions.e: The five permanent members, the US, Russia, UK, France and China, each have a veto.

questions.q: The first Secretary-General of the United Nations was ______.
questions.e: Trygve Lie of Norway was the first UN Secretary-General (1946-52).

questions.q: How many member states does the United Nations have?
questions.e: The UN began with 51 members in 1945 and now has 193 member states.

questions.q: The UN Security Council has permanent and non-permanent members, and the UN family includes many other organisations.
p: (a) How many non-permanent members does the Security Council have?
(b) For how many years are the non-permanent members elected?
years
(c) In which city does the World Trade Organisation have its headquarters?
Geneva
questions.e: The 10 non-permanent members are elected for two years at a time; the WTO, set up in 1995, is based in Geneva.

questions.q: The 1968 treaty that allowed only five countries to keep nuclear weapons and aimed to stop their spread is the ______.
questions.a: NPT|Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty|Non-Proliferation Treaty|Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons
questions.e: The NPT (1968) recognised only five nuclear weapon states; India refused to sign it, calling it discriminatory.

questions.q: The Chemical Weapons Convention, which bans the making and possession of chemical weapons, was agreed in ______.
questions.e: The Chemical Weapons Convention of 1992 and the Biological Weapons Convention of 1972 are examples of disarmament.

questions.q: The concept that security should focus on the protection of people rather than of territories or states is called ______.
questions.e: Human security aims to protect individuals from threats like violence, hunger and disease.

questions.q: Threats such as terrorism, global poverty, health epidemics and migration fall under the ______ notion of security.
questions.e: Non-traditional security goes beyond military threats to include dangers to human existence and well-being.

questions.q: The UN Conference on Environment and Development (Earth Summit) of 1992 was held at ______.
questions.e: The Rio Earth Summit (1992) produced conventions on climate change and biodiversity and Agenda 21.

questions.q: The Kyoto Protocol, setting targets for industrialised countries to cut greenhouse gas emissions, was agreed in ______.
questions.e: The Kyoto Protocol was agreed in Japan in 1997 under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.

questions.q: The principle that developed countries should bear more responsibility for protecting the global environment is called 'common but ______ responsibilities'.
questions.e: Since developed countries caused most pollution historically, they are expected to do more; India supports this principle.

questions.q: Areas outside the sovereign jurisdiction of any one state, such as Antarctica, outer space and the ocean floor, are called the global ______.
questions.e: The global commons require international cooperation, for example the Antarctic Treaty of 1959.

questions.q: Concern for the environment has become part of world politics since the 1980s.
p: (a) What was the title of the report of the Brundtland Commission?
Our Common Future
(b) In which year was this report published?
(c) In which year did India ratify (accede to) the Kyoto Protocol?
questions.e: 'Our Common Future' (1987) warned against traditional patterns of growth; India acceded to (ratified) the Kyoto Protocol in August 2002.

questions.q: The first meeting of the World Social Forum, a platform against neo-liberal globalisation, was held at Porto Alegre in 2001 in which country?
questions.e: The World Social Forum brings together activists opposed to neo-liberal globalisation; its first meeting was in Porto Alegre, Brazil.

questions.q: India began its new economic policy of liberalisation in ______.
questions.e: In 1991, responding to a financial crisis, India began economic reforms and opened up to the global economy.

questions.q: The fourth meeting of the World Social Forum was held in which Indian city in 2004?
questions.e: The fourth WSF meeting was held in Mumbai in January 2004.

questions.q: The fear that globalisation spreads the culture of the dominant power across the world, making all cultures alike, is described as cultural ______.
questions.e: Cultural homogenisation, sometimes called McDonaldisation, is the spread of a dominant Western culture, while heterogenisation makes cultures more varied.

questions.q: Which Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister led the integration of the princely states into India?
questions.e: Sardar Patel used persuasion and firmness to bring almost all princely states into the Indian Union.

questions.q: The States Reorganisation Commission was appointed in ______.
questions.e: The Commission, appointed in 1953, accepted linguistic boundaries; the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 created 14 states and 6 union territories.

questions.q: Whose death in December 1952, after a fast of 56 days, forced the government to announce a separate Andhra state?
questions.e: Potti Sriramulu's death led to violent protests, and Andhra state was formed in 1953.

questions.q: Which princely state, ruled by the Nizam, was integrated into India after military action in September 1948?
questions.e: After the Nizam resisted, the Indian army moved in in September 1948 and Hyderabad acceded to India.

questions.q: After independence the princely states had to be integrated and state boundaries redrawn.
p: (a) What was the document by which most princely rulers agreed to join India called?
Instrument of Accession
(b) In which year did the Maharaja of Manipur sign the Merger Agreement with India?
(c) In which year was Bombay state divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat?
questions.e: Rulers signed the Instrument of Accession; Manipur's Maharaja signed the Merger Agreement in September 1949; Maharashtra and Gujarat were created in 1960.

questions.q: The Planning Commission of India was set up in ______.
questions.e: The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950 by a simple resolution of the Government of India, with the Prime Minister as its chairperson.

questions.q: Which young economist was involved in drafting the First Five Year Plan (1951-56) and argued that India should 'hasten slowly'?
questions.e: K.N. Raj argued that India should 'hasten slowly' for the first two decades; the plan focused on agriculture and dams.

questions.q: The Second Five Year Plan, which stressed heavy industries, was drafted under the leadership of the economist and statistician ______.
questions.e: The Mahalanobis plan aimed at quick structural change through heavy industrialisation.

questions.q: In which year did the NITI Aayog replace the Planning Commission?
questions.e: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was set up on 1 January 2015 in place of the Planning Commission.

questions.q: The Panchsheel, five principles of peaceful coexistence, was signed in 1954 between India and ______.
questions.e: Nehru and Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai signed the Panchsheel on 29 April 1954.

questions.q: The Afro-Asian conference of 1955, which led to the Non-Aligned Movement, was held at Bandung in ______.
questions.e: The Bandung Conference of 1955 marked the high point of India's engagement with newly independent Asian and African nations.

questions.q: After the 1965 war, Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri signed the Tashkent Agreement (1966) with Pakistan's President ______.
questions.a: Ayub Khan|General Ayub Khan|Muhammad Ayub Khan|Mohammad Ayub Khan
questions.e: The Tashkent Agreement was brokered by the Soviet Union in January 1966.

questions.q: India's foreign policy saw several major events in the early 1970s.
p: (a) Where did India conduct its first nuclear test in May 1974?
Pokhran|Pokharan
(b) In which year did India sign the 20-year Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the Soviet Union?
(c) With which Pakistani leader did Indira Gandhi sign the Simla Agreement in 1972?
Zulfikar Ali Bhutto|Bhutto|Z.A. Bhutto|ZA Bhutto
questions.e: India signed the Indo-Soviet treaty in August 1971, the Simla Agreement with Bhutto in 1972, and conducted a nuclear test at Pokhran in 1974.

questions.q: The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement was held in 1961 at ______.
questions.e: The first NAM summit in Belgrade (1961) was co-founded by Nehru, Tito and Nasser.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: Who was elected Prime Minister after Nehru's death in 1964?
questions.e: Lal Bahadur Shastri became Prime Minister in 1964 and gave the slogan 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan'.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: Indira Gandhi's famous slogan in the 1971 Lok Sabha elections was ______.
questions.e: 'Garibi Hatao' gave Indira Gandhi's Congress a massive victory in 1971; the opposition's slogan was 'Indira Hatao'.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: In the 1969 presidential election, Indira Gandhi backed which candidate against the official Congress candidate N. Sanjeeva Reddy?
questions.e: V.V. Giri won after Indira Gandhi called for a 'conscience vote'; the Congress split soon afterwards.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: The phrase 'Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram', used for frequent defections, arose from the actions of an MLA, Gaya Lal, in 1967 in which state?
questions.e: Gaya Lal of Haryana changed parties three times in a fortnight in 1967, giving rise to the phrase.

questions.q: The founder of the Bolshevik Communist Party, who led the revolution of 1917 in Russia, was ______.
questions.e: Lenin led the Bolshevik revolution of 1917 and was the architect of the early Soviet state.

questions.q: Which leader opposed the coup by communist hardliners in August 1991 and emerged as a national hero in Russia?
questions.e: Boris Yeltsin, elected President of Russia in 1991, led the resistance to the coup and then the move away from the Soviet system.

questions.q: Which leader, Lenin's successor, led the Soviet Union from 1924 to 1953?
questions.e: Stalin led the Soviet Union during its consolidation, with rapid industrialisation and forcible collectivisation of agriculture.

questions.q: The Soviet political system was dominated by a single party, the ______ Party.
questions.a: Communist|Communist Party of the Soviet Union
questions.e: The one-party system of the Communist Party allowed no other party and was not accountable to the people.

questions.q: In the Soviet system, the economy was planned and controlled by the ______.
questions.e: The Soviet system gave primacy to the state: ownership and control of the means of production were with the state.

questions.q: Which country did the Soviet Union intervene in militarily in 1979, an action that weakened the Soviet system?
questions.e: The intervention in Afghanistan in 1979 strained the Soviet economy and system.

questions.q: After the disintegration of the USSR, Russia inherited the Soviet seat in the ______.
questions.a: UN Security Council|Security Council|UNSC|United Nations Security Council
questions.e: Russia was accepted as the successor state of the Soviet Union and took over its permanent seat in the Security Council.

questions.q: Because valuable state industries were sold at very low prices under shock therapy, the episode has been called the largest ______ sale in history.
questions.e: About 90 per cent of Russian industries were offered for sale to private individuals and companies at throwaway prices.

questions.q: Chechnya and Dagestan, which have seen violent secessionist movements, are regions of ______.
questions.e: Several post-Soviet states faced conflicts; in Russia, Chechnya and Dagestan had violent secessionist movements.

questions.q: Which Central Asian republic went through a civil war that lasted ten years, until 2001?
questions.e: NCERT notes that Tajikistan witnessed a civil war that went on for ten years, till 2001; the Central Asian region saw tensions after the Soviet break-up.

questions.q: The Soviet Union faced growing pressure for change in the 1980s and early 1990s.
p: (a) In which year did Mikhail Gorbachev become General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union?
(b) Boris Yeltsin was elected President of which Soviet republic in 1991?
Russia
(c) Which Baltic republic was the first of the 15 Soviet republics to declare independence, in March 1990?
Lithuania
questions.e: Gorbachev took over in 1985; Lithuania declared independence in March 1990; Yeltsin was elected President of Russia in June 1991.

questions.q: The common currency used by many members of the European Union is the ______.
questions.e: The euro was introduced in 1999 for accounting and as notes and coins in 2002; it is a symbol of the EU's economic power.

questions.q: ASEAN stands for the Association of ______ Asian Nations.
questions.e: ASEAN was set up in 1967 by five Southeast Asian countries; it now has ten members.

questions.q: The People's Republic of China was established after the Communist revolution of 1949 under the leadership of ______.
questions.e: After 1949 China followed the Soviet model of a state-controlled economy until the reforms of 1978.

questions.q: The European Economic Community was created in ______.
questions.e: The EEC (1957) acquired a political dimension with the creation of the European Parliament, and became the European Union in 1992.

questions.q: The ASEAN Regional Forum, which coordinates security and foreign policy, was established in ______.
questions.e: The ARF (1994) carries out coordination of security and foreign policy among ASEAN members and partners.

questions.q: ASEAN's informal, non-confrontational and cooperative style of interaction is known as the ______.
questions.e: The ASEAN Way respects national sovereignty and prefers consensus over confrontation.

questions.q: The flag of the European Union has a circle of how many gold stars?
questions.e: The circle of twelve gold stars stands for solidarity and harmony among the peoples of Europe; it does not represent the number of members.

questions.q: The ASEAN Community rests on three pillars: the ASEAN Security Community, the ASEAN Economic Community and the ASEAN ______ Community.
questions.e: In 2003 ASEAN moved to establish an ASEAN Community with these three pillars.

questions.q: Through which American plan, announced after the Second World War, did the USA give massive financial help to revive Europe's economy?
questions.e: The Marshall Plan led to the Organisation for European Economic Cooperation in 1948 and helped start European cooperation.

questions.q: The organisation set up in 1948 to channel Marshall Plan aid to the West European states was the ______.
questions.a: Organisation for European Economic Cooperation|Organization for European Economic Cooperation|OEEC
questions.e: The OEEC became a forum where the Western European states began to cooperate on trade and economic issues.

questions.q: In China, privatisation of agriculture in 1982 was followed by privatisation of industry in ______.
questions.e: China followed a phased approach: agriculture in 1982, industry in 1998, with trade barriers removed only in Special Economic Zones.

questions.q: The European Union has started to act like a nation state: it has its own flag, anthem, founding date and ______.
questions.e: The EU has its own flag, anthem, founding date and currency (the euro), and a common foreign and security policy.

questions.q: China's economy was transformed after the reforms announced in 1978.
p: (a) In which year was agriculture privatised in China?
(b) What are the zones where China removed trade barriers to attract foreign investors called?
Special Economic Zones|SEZ|SEZs|Special Economic Zone
(c) In which year did China join the World Trade Organisation?
questions.e: China privatised agriculture in 1982, set up Special Economic Zones for foreign investment, and joined the WTO in 2001.

questions.q: Which South Asian country was a sultanate until 1968, when it became a republic with a presidential form of government?
questions.e: The Maldives became a republic in 1968 and introduced a multi-party system in 2005.

questions.q: The South Asian Free Trade Agreement (SAFTA) was signed by the SAARC members in ______.
questions.e: SAFTA was signed in 2004 and came into effect on 1 January 2006, aiming to lower trade tariffs in the region.

questions.q: Which leader of the Awami League led the popular struggle of East Pakistan against West Pakistani domination?
questions.a: Sheikh Mujib-ur Rahman|Sheikh Mujibur Rahman|Mujibur Rahman|Sheikh Mujib|Mujib
questions.e: Sheikh Mujib led the struggle that ended in the creation of Bangladesh in 1971 and became its first leader.

questions.q: India sent the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) to Sri Lanka in ______.
questions.e: The IPKF was sent in 1987 after an accord between India and Sri Lanka; it was withdrawn in 1989-90.

questions.q: Which military ruler took over Pakistan in 1977 after a popular movement against the government of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto?
questions.e: General Zia-ul-Haq ruled until 1988; a pro-democracy movement followed and elected governments returned.

questions.q: Soon after Pakistan framed its first constitution, which general took over the administration of the country?
questions.a: Ayub Khan|General Ayub Khan|Muhammad Ayub Khan|Mohammad Ayub Khan
questions.e: General Ayub Khan soon got himself elected; popular unrest forced him out and General Yahya Khan took over.

questions.q: Which army general removed Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and took over the government of Pakistan in 1999?
questions.e: General Musharraf took over in 1999 and later got himself elected President.

questions.q: Sheikh Mujib-ur Rahman was assassinated in a military uprising in ______.
questions.e: Mujib was killed in August 1975 after he had abolished other parties and set up a presidential form of government.

questions.q: The Maldives introduced a multi-party system in ______.
questions.e: In 2005 the Maldives parliament voted overwhelmingly to introduce a multi-party system.

questions.q: In Sri Lanka, the majority community that dominated politics after independence and was accused of neglecting Tamil interests is the ______ community.
questions.e: Sinhala nationalism led to tensions with Sri Lankan Tamils, many of whom had roots in India, and later to the LTTE's armed struggle.

questions.q: The countries of South Asia have taken steps towards regional cooperation.
p: (a) How many member countries does SAARC have?
(b) In which year did SAFTA come into effect?
questions.e: SAARC has eight members: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka; SAFTA came into effect on 1 January 2006.

questions.q: In which city are the headquarters of the United Nations?
questions.e: The UN headquarters is in New York; several UN bodies are based in Geneva.

questions.q: UN Day is celebrated every year on 24 ______.
questions.e: The UN was established on 24 October 1945, so 24 October is celebrated as UN Day.

questions.q: The international organisation that sets the rules for global trade, set up in 1995, is the ______.
questions.e: The WTO, which succeeded GATT, sets the rules of global trade so that trade flows smoothly and freely.

questions.q: How many countries were founding members of the United Nations in 1945?
questions.e: The UN began with 51 member states; it now has 193.

questions.q: The power of each permanent member of the UN Security Council to block a decision is called the ______.
questions.e: A negative vote by any one of the five permanent members stops a Security Council decision.

questions.q: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which promotes the peaceful use of nuclear energy, was established in ______.
questions.e: The IAEA was set up in 1957; its inspectors visit nuclear facilities to check that they are used for peaceful purposes.

questions.q: The World Bank was created in ______.
questions.e: The World Bank was created in 1945; it works on human development, agriculture, environment, infrastructure and governance.

questions.q: Which South Korean diplomat was Secretary-General of the United Nations from 2007 to 2016?
questions.e: Ban Ki-moon served two terms as UN Secretary-General, succeeding Kofi Annan.

questions.q: Kofi Annan, UN Secretary-General from 1997 to 2006, was from which country?
questions.e: Kofi Annan of Ghana was the seventh Secretary-General; he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2001 along with the UN.

questions.q: Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch are examples of ______ that work on human rights.
questions.e: These non-governmental organisations draw attention to human rights abuses across the world.

questions.q: Several international organisations deal with the world economy.
p: (a) Which organisation oversees international financial institutions and regulations?
IMF|International Monetary Fund
(b) In which year was the World Trade Organisation set up?
(c) The WTO was set up as the successor to which agreement?
GATT|General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
questions.e: The IMF oversees international financial institutions; the WTO was set up in 1995 as the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT).

questions.q: The Biological Weapons Convention, which bans the making and possession of biological weapons, was signed in ______.
questions.e: The BWC (1972) and the Chemical Weapons Convention (1992) are examples of disarmament agreements.

questions.q: In the traditional conception of security, the greatest danger to a country is from ______ threats.
questions.e: Traditional security focuses on the use or threat of military force by another country.

questions.q: People who flee their own country because of war, persecution or disaster and seek protection in another country are called ______.
questions.e: Refugees cross national borders; people who flee their homes but stay within their own country are internally displaced.

questions.q: Terrorism refers to political violence that deliberately and indiscriminately targets ______.
questions.e: Terrorists aim to coerce a political community by using or threatening violence against ordinary people.

questions.q: A coalition of states that coordinate their actions to deter or defend against military attack is called an ______.
questions.e: Alliance building is a component of traditional security policy; alliances are formalised in written treaties.

questions.q: The 1972 treaty that stopped the USA and the USSR from using ballistic missiles as a defensive shield to launch a nuclear attack was the ______ Treaty.
questions.e: The ABM Treaty is an example of arms control between the two superpowers.

questions.q: Preventing any one country from becoming so powerful that it threatens others is called maintaining the balance of ______.
questions.e: Governments are sensitive to the balance of power between their country and others, especially neighbours.

questions.q: Regulating the acquisition or development of weapons, rather than abolishing them, is called arms ______.
questions.e: Arms control regulates weapons (for example the ABM Treaty), while disarmament requires states to give up certain kinds of weapons.

questions.q: Exchanging information on military matters and on the timing of military exercises are examples of ______-building measures.
questions.e: Confidence building is a process in which countries share information to avoid violent conflict through misunderstanding.

questions.q: People who have fled their homes but remain within their own national borders are called internally ______ people.
questions.e: Unlike refugees, internally displaced people do not cross an international border.

questions.q: Threats from within a country's own borders, such as armed secessionist movements, are the concern of ______ security.
questions.e: Traditional security deals with both external threats and internal security, that is, peace and order within the state.

questions.q: Traditional security policy uses different strategies against the threat of war.
p: (a) The policy concerned with preventing war is called ______.
deterrence
(b) The policy concerned with limiting or ending war is called ______.
defence|defense
(c) Requiring all states to give up certain kinds of weapons is called ______.
disarmament
questions.e: Deterrence aims to prevent war, defence aims to limit or end it, and disarmament requires states to give up certain weapons, as under the BWC and CWC.

questions.q: The book 'Limits to Growth', published in 1972, was brought out by the ______.
questions.e: It warned of the potential depletion of the earth's resources against the background of rapidly growing world population.

questions.q: The Kyoto Protocol on cutting greenhouse gas emissions was agreed in which country?
questions.e: The protocol was agreed at Kyoto in Japan in 1997, based on principles set out in the UNFCCC.

questions.q: The Antarctic Treaty, which deals with one of the global commons, was signed in ______.
questions.e: The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 was followed by the Montreal Protocol (1987) and the Antarctic Environmental Protocol (1991).

questions.q: The Montreal Protocol aims to protect the earth's ______ layer.
questions.e: The thinning of the ozone layer, the ozone hole, threatens ecosystems and human health.

questions.q: The list of development practices adopted at the 1992 Earth Summit is called ______.
questions.e: Agenda 21 recommended development practices for achieving sustainable development.

questions.q: Patches of forest protected by local communities in India for religious reasons are called ______ groves.
questions.e: Sacred groves reflect traditional community conservation practices that protect forests outside state control.

questions.q: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was adopted in ______.
questions.e: The UNFCCC (1992) laid down the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities; the Kyoto Protocol followed in 1997.

questions.q: The approach agreed at Rio in 1992, which combines economic growth with ecological responsibility, is called ______ development.
questions.e: Sustainable development meets the needs of the present without harming the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

questions.q: Under the Kyoto Protocol, India, China and other ______ countries were exempt from binding requirements to reduce emissions.
questions.e: This reflects the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, since developing countries contributed little to historic emissions.

questions.q: Descendants of the people who lived in a territory before others settled there, such as the Adivasis in India, are called ______ peoples.
questions.e: Indigenous peoples' rights to their land and resources are an issue in global environmental politics.

questions.q: International agreements have been made to protect the global commons.
p: (a) In which year was the Montreal Protocol signed?
(b) In which year was the Antarctic Environmental Protocol signed?
questions.e: The Montreal Protocol (1987) and the Antarctic Environmental Protocol (1991) followed the Antarctic Treaty of 1959.

questions.q: Globalisation involves flows of ideas, capital, commodities and ______ across different parts of the world.
questions.e: Globalisation is about worldwide flows, and the structures that keep them going.

questions.q: Advances in ______, such as the telegraph, telephone, microchip and internet, have been a critical cause of globalisation.
questions.e: Technology has made it possible for ideas, capital, commodities and people to move much more easily.

questions.q: Companies that operate in more than one country, such as large car makers, are called ______.
questions.e: The growing role of MNCs reduces the ability of governments to take decisions on their own.

questions.q: Critics argue that under globalisation, the ______ replaces the state as the main determinant of economic and social priorities.
questions.e: As the welfare state gives way to a minimalist state, the market becomes the prime determinant of priorities.

questions.q: To protect the poor from the harmful effects of globalisation, some argue for social ______ nets.
questions.e: Social safety nets aim to reduce the ill effects of economic globalisation on the economically weak.

questions.q: When external influences enlarge choices and make cultures more varied, the process is called cultural ______.
questions.e: Not all external influences are bad; blue jeans, for example, sit alongside the khadi kurta, showing heterogenisation.

questions.q: Globalisation as a concept fundamentally deals with flows that create world-wide ______.
questions.e: These flows of ideas, capital, commodities and people create world-wide interconnectedness.

questions.q: The spread of a uniform Western culture through globalisation, named after a fast food chain, is sometimes called ______.
questions.e: Critics fear that this cultural homogenisation threatens traditional cultures across the world.

questions.q: The open platform that brings together human rights activists, environmentalists, labour, youth and women activists opposed to neo-liberal globalisation is the ______.
questions.e: The WSF first met at Porto Alegre, Brazil, in 2001; its fourth meeting was held in Mumbai in 2004.

questions.q: One view holds that globalisation results in an erosion of state ______, that is, the ability of governments to do what they do.
questions.e: The old welfare state gives way to a minimalist state that performs only core functions such as law and order and security.

questions.q: Movement of people across countries has not grown as fast as flows of goods and capital, because developed countries have carefully guarded their ______ with visa policies.
questions.e: Globalisation is uneven: the movement of people is much more restricted than the movement of goods and capital.

questions.q: Globalisation has met with strong resistance across the world.
p: (a) In which year was the first meeting of the World Social Forum held?
(b) In which city were there widespread protests at the WTO Ministerial Meeting of 1999?
Seattle
questions.e: Protests at Seattle in 1999 targeted unfair trading practices; the World Social Forum first met at Porto Alegre in 2001.

questions.q: India became independent at midnight on 14-15 August ______.
questions.e: Independence came along with the partition of the country into India and Pakistan.

questions.q: Jawaharlal Nehru's speech to the Constituent Assembly at midnight on 14-15 August 1947 is known as '______ with Destiny'.
questions.e: In the speech Nehru spoke of India keeping its 'tryst with destiny' at the moment of independence.

questions.q: Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated on 30 January 1948 by ______.
questions.e: Gandhi's death had an almost magical effect on the communal situation in the country.

questions.q: The theory advanced by the Muslim League that India consisted of two separate peoples, Hindus and Muslims, is called the ______ theory.
questions.e: Partition was based on this theory, which the Congress opposed.

questions.q: Which leader of the North West Frontier Province, known as 'Frontier Gandhi', opposed the two-nation theory?
questions.a: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan|Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan|Abdul Ghaffar Khan|Abdul Gaffar Khan|Ghaffar Khan|Gaffar Khan|Badshah Khan
questions.e: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan was a Gandhian leader of the Pathans; his province was nevertheless merged with Pakistan.

questions.q: According to NCERT, how many princely states were there in British India at the time of independence?
questions.e: Almost all of the 565 princely states agreed to join India by signing the Instrument of Accession.

questions.q: Which princely state, whose Nawab wanted to join Pakistan, was integrated with India after a plebiscite confirmed the people's wish to join India?
questions.e: Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir and Manipur were more difficult to integrate than the other states.

questions.q: In June 1948, which princely state became the first part of India to hold an election under universal adult franchise?
questions.e: The Maharaja of Manipur held elections and the state became a constitutional monarchy; it merged with India in 1949.

questions.q: The Nizam's paramilitary force that unleashed atrocities against the people of Hyderabad was called the ______.
questions.e: The Razakars targeted non-Muslims and the peasant movement; the Indian army moved in in September 1948.

questions.q: Which state was carved out of Punjab in 1966?
questions.e: In 1966 Punjab was reorganised and Haryana was created as a separate state.

questions.q: The map of India's states continued to change after the reorganisation of 1956.
p: (a) In which year was Nagaland created as a state?
(b) In which year were Uttarakhand, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand created?
(c) In which year was Telangana created out of Andhra Pradesh?
questions.e: Nagaland became a state in 1963; Uttarakhand, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand were created in 2000; Telangana was created in 2014.

questions.q: The First Five Year Plan (1951-56) focused mainly on ______.
questions.e: It gave priority to agriculture, including investment in dams and irrigation, and land reforms.

questions.q: The plan for a planned economy drawn up in 1944 by a section of big industrialists is called the ______ Plan.
questions.e: The Bombay Plan wanted the state to take major initiatives in industrial and other economic investments.

questions.q: An economy in which both the public sector and the private sector play important roles, as India chose after independence, is called a ______ economy.
questions.e: India followed a mixed economy model with a large public sector alongside private enterprise.

questions.q: Who is called the 'Milkman of India' for his role in the Amul cooperative and Operation Flood?
questions.e: Kurien led the cooperative dairy movement at Anand in Gujarat, which grew into the White Revolution.

questions.q: The Green Revolution mainly benefited regions with good irrigation, such as Punjab, Haryana and western ______.
questions.e: The use of high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation raised wheat output especially in these areas, but widened regional disparities.

questions.q: The Gandhian economist J.C. Kumarappa set out an alternative strategy of development in his book 'Economy of ______'.
questions.e: Kumarappa argued for a rural-centred, Gandhian approach to development.

questions.q: After the Third Five Year Plan, there was a 'plan holiday', and the Fourth Plan started only in ______.
questions.e: The Fourth Plan was due to start in 1966, but war, drought and economic crisis led to a plan holiday until 1969.

questions.q: Which leader, later Prime Minister, argued forcefully that agriculture and the rural poor should be at the centre of planning?
questions.a: Charan Singh|Chaudhary Charan Singh|Chaudhury Charan Singh
questions.e: Charan Singh criticised the stress on heavy industry and urban development in planning.

questions.q: Which state's model of development, focusing on education, health, land reform and poverty alleviation, became well known as an alternative to growth-led development?
questions.e: The Kerala model achieved high levels of literacy and health despite low per capita income.

questions.q: Which colonial system of landholding, under which landlords collected rent from cultivators, was abolished as a major land reform after independence?
questions.e: The abolition of zamindari freed land from the control of a class with little interest in agriculture.

questions.q: Which Five Year Plan, drafted under P.C. Mahalanobis, began in 1956?
questions.e: The Second Plan (1956-61) stressed heavy industry, unlike the agriculture-focused First Plan (1951-56).

questions.q: The Planning Commission guided India's development for more than six decades.
p: (a) Who was the first chairperson of the Planning Commission?
Jawaharlal Nehru|Nehru
(b) Which body replaced the Planning Commission?
NITI Aayog|NITI|National Institution for Transforming India
questions.e: The Prime Minister, first Jawaharlal Nehru, chaired the Planning Commission; it was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.

questions.q: India and China fought a border war in ______.
questions.e: The Chinese attack of October 1962 on both the eastern and western fronts was a setback for India's image and for Nehru.

questions.q: Which Prime Minister was also India's foreign minister from 1946 to 1964 and shaped its foreign policy?
questions.e: Nehru, as Prime Minister and foreign minister, set the agenda of non-alignment.

questions.q: The Kargil conflict between India and Pakistan took place in ______.
questions.e: In 1999 Indian forces responded to infiltration across the Line of Control in the Kargil sector.

questions.q: Which Tibetan spiritual leader was given political asylum in India in 1959?
questions.a: Dalai Lama|the Dalai Lama|14th Dalai Lama
questions.e: The Dalai Lama's asylum in 1959 was one of the issues that strained relations between India and China.

questions.q: The boundary between India and China in the eastern sector is known as the ______ Line.
questions.e: China disputed the McMahon Line and claimed much of the territory in the eastern sector (then NEFA).

questions.q: The disputed area in the western sector of the India-China border, in Ladakh, is ______.
questions.e: The boundary dispute concerned Aksai Chin in the western sector and much of present-day Arunachal Pradesh in the eastern sector.

questions.q: Which Defence Minister had to leave the Cabinet after India's defeat in the 1962 war?
questions.a: V.K. Krishna Menon|Krishna Menon|VK Krishna Menon|V K Krishna Menon|Menon
questions.e: The 1962 war led to criticism of the government; Krishna Menon left the Cabinet.

questions.q: India's nuclear doctrine commits the country to no ______ use of nuclear weapons.
questions.e: India's doctrine of credible minimum deterrence professes 'no first use' and global, verifiable disarmament.

questions.q: The North East Frontier Agency (NEFA), much of which China claimed during the 1962 conflict, is today the state of ______.
questions.e: China claimed most of the area of NEFA in the eastern sector.

questions.q: In which year did the first war between India and Pakistan over Kashmir break out?
questions.e: Soon after partition, a proxy war broke out in Kashmir in 1947; the conflict ended with a ceasefire.

questions.q: India has followed an independent nuclear policy.
p: (a) Under which Prime Minister did India conduct its first nuclear test in 1974?
Indira Gandhi|Indira
(b) In which year did India carry out a series of nuclear tests at Pokhran?
questions.e: India's first nuclear test took place in May 1974 under Indira Gandhi; in May 1998 it conducted further tests, demonstrating its nuclear weapons capability.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: Which slogan did Lal Bahadur Shastri give during the 1965 war with Pakistan?
questions.a: Jai Jawan Jai Kisan|Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan
questions.e: The slogan symbolised his resolve to face both the war and the food crisis.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: In January 1966, Lal Bahadur Shastri died suddenly at ______.
questions.e: Shastri died in Tashkent (then in the USSR, now in Uzbekistan) soon after signing the Tashkent Agreement with Pakistan.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: After Shastri's death in 1966, who defeated Morarji Desai in the contest among Congress MPs to become Prime Minister?
questions.e: Indira Gandhi won the contest with the support of the senior leaders known as the Syndicate.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: The group of powerful Congress leaders who controlled the party organisation in the 1960s was informally called the ______.
questions.e: The Syndicate included K. Kamaraj, S.K. Patil, S. Nijalingappa, N. Sanjeeva Reddy and Atulya Ghosh.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: The socialist leader who gave the strategy of 'non-Congressism' was ______.
questions.e: Lohia argued that Congress rule was undemocratic and that opposition parties should come together against it.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: In 1967, the DMK came to power in Madras state under the leadership of ______.
questions.e: Annadurai became Chief Minister of Madras in 1967; the DMK had gained popularity from the anti-Hindi agitation.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: Which Congress President, a leader from Tamil Nadu, played a key role as 'kingmaker' in the choice of Shastri as Prime Minister?
questions.e: Kamaraj, a former Chief Minister of Madras, was Congress President in the 1960s and a leading member of the Syndicate.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: After the split of 1969, the Congress faction led by the Syndicate came to be known as the Congress (______).
questions.e: The Syndicate's group was called Congress (Organisation) and Indira Gandhi's group Congress (Requisitionists).

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: In July 1969, the government nationalised how many leading private banks?
questions.e: Bank nationalisation was part of Indira Gandhi's left-leaning programme, along with the abolition of the privy purse.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: The 1967 elections, in which the Congress lost its majority in many states, have been described as a political ______.
questions.e: The Congress just about retained its majority in the Lok Sabha and lost power in many states.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: The coalition governments formed by non-Congress parties in several states after 1967 were called ______ governments.
questions.e: SVD governments brought together parties with very different ideologies against the Congress.

questions.t: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
questions.q: The 1971 Lok Sabha election restored the dominance of the Congress.
p: (a) How many Lok Sabha seats did the Congress (R) win on its own?
(b) Which party was the Congress (R)'s ally in this election?
CPI|Communist Party of India
(c) What was the alliance of the main non-communist, non-Congress opposition parties called?
Grand Alliance|the Grand Alliance
questions.e: The Congress (R)-CPI alliance won 375 seats, with the Congress (R) alone winning 352; the Grand Alliance included the Congress (O), the Jana Sangh, the Swatantra Party and others.
